segments.description: Hi, everyone. It's an absolute honour to be hosting this Q&A with Australia's very own Stephen Huss. Stephen is the 2005 Wimbledon Doubles Champion, former World No. 22 and revered Auburn Tigers US College player. Former USTA, National Women's High Performance Coach. At present, he's the director of 7576 in Atlanta, Georgia. Check that out on Facebook. Former Melbourneian, super humble, all-round nice guy. You're in for a treat today as Stephen regards us with athlete-centred coaching. Steve, how are you? I'm doing great, Paul. How are you today? Good. Thanks, mate. And they tell me in Atlanta, Georgia it's minus three degrees. It's cold. It's probably not quite that cold at the moment, but we've had snow in the last couple of days. So, yeah, it's a little chilly. Yeah, indeed. Look, let's get right into your presentation. Your definition of athlete-centred coaching is phenomenal. And it can often be glossed over, always doing things in the best interest of the athlete. And it's easy for the ego of the coach and even parents to get involved. I mean, it could be. I don't believe that coaches intentionally would make decisions that are not in the best interest of the athlete. I think that the challenge comes is perhaps when they make a decision emotionally or under some stress, or perhaps they haven't gained enough experience or knowledge to make a good informed decision around the athlete.

So, I'm not sure anyone intentionally does it, but it does happen from time to time. And so my message would just be to take all the information you can and try and process it and don't make a quick reactive decision and then act in the best interest of the athlete. So, I don't think it's necessarily ego that overtakes us. It could be some other things. Yeah, indeed. But, yeah, take your time and make an informed decision. Yeah. In club coaching, and certainly what a lot of coaches who might be watching this presentation, when would it be appropriate to use a more autocratic coaching style? So, IE when the player can't properly appreciate their own agency. Yeah, like a young child, for example. Yeah, I mean, I do believe that good coaches and good leaders can sort of shift between leadership styles, so they're not one way all the time. And certainly autocratic is a leadership style. I think it's becoming less and less popular. You even hear, you know, some revered and great coaches like Wayne Bennett. I can think of an all blacks coach that I've done a lot of research on. His name is slipping me right now, but who's kind of changed their ways to be a lot less autocratic. So, I don't think that's as popular anymore, but it's certainly true that the younger an athlete is or a child is, the less independence you can give them and the more direct instruction you need to give them.

I mean, I can't say I believe in you if a player is not, you know, is not progressing is not having results but is not giving effort either. You know, like so, but you can say to a player hey, if we show up I know if we show up for the next 10 sessions, and you give great effort and we get the repetitions in. I know you're going to get better and I believe in you and I believe that your serves going to get better so let's do that and let's start the work. Not only my coaching but from my personal experience of a mentor of mine sort of taken me aside at a very important time and showing what I needed at that point in my life when I was in my late teens and just showing me I believe in you we're going to do this work and I'm with you. And that can be incredibly powerful so I don't think you need the success as a precursor to say I believe in you. It certainly helps, but I you know confidence comes from those little achievements and it comes from the results that you get for sure. And I truly believe that confidence comes from your most recent experiences and the preparation and the work you do helps you sort of get better in that area, but ultimately you need to have those little successes for confidence but we don't need those successes to say hey I believe in you.
